This consistency across systems strengthens and supports our conclusion of structural re-organization driven by hydration. While Kamlet-Taft parameters provide useful semi-empirical insight into solvent polarity and hydrogen bonding, it is important to note their limitations in structured or heterogeneous systems like DES-water mixtures. The measured values reflect the local environment of the solvatochromic dye, which may be partitioned into specific domains and not fully represent the bulk properties of the solvent. As such, these parameters should be interpreted as qualitative indicators of solvation trends rather than absolute descriptors of the entire system. For this reason, the solvatochromic data were complemented by molecular dynamics simulations, which offer a more physically grounded view of intermolecular interactions and network reorganization. Indeed, as observed in both experimental and theoretical studies, water initially integrates into the DES matrix, occupying available hydrogen-bonding sites and gradually modifying its physicochemical properties. However, beyond a critical hydration level—consistent with the 67 mol% water thresholds identified here—disruptions in the hydrogen-bond network become more pronounced, leading to structural rearrangements such as cluster formation, as seen in MD simulations. This transition reinforces the idea that, at high hydration levels, DES properties evolve into an aqueous-like system, supporting the concept of a DES-in-water regime, suggesting a fundamental shift in solvation dynamics at high water content. These findings demonstrate that water plays an active role in modulating the solvation environment, influencing both extraction efficiency and solvent behavior at the molecular level. ## 4. Concluding remarks This study provides a comprehensive understanding at the molecular level of the transition between _water-in-DES_ to _DES-in-water_ and its impact on the extraction of polyphenol. Through a combined experimental and theoretical approach, we demonstrate that water plays a dual role: initially integrating into the DES structure, stabilizing the hydrogen-bond network, and optimizing extraction properties, but eventually disrupting this organization at higher concentrations. Our findings show that DES maintains its structure up to 67 mol% water, with water modulating viscosity and solvation. However, beyond this threshold, a shift occurs characterized by the formation of choline-lactic acid clusters sur- Journal of Molecular Liquids 436 (2025) 128124 rounded by non-interacting water, as evidenced by TGA, RDF, and KT parameters. This structural evolution directly influences the extraction efficiency of polyphenols. While a well-balanced DES-water mixture enhances the solubility and mass transfer, excessive water disrupts the DES frame-work, altering its physicochemical properties and leading to an aqueous-like system. Polyphenol extraction becomes efficient again in highly hy-drated systems, suggesting that DES composition changes, contributing to solvation dynamics despite the predominant aqueous environment. This finding reveals the complex interplay between solvent composition and extraction performance, highlighting the need for further investiga-tion into the specific mechanisms and structures at the molecular level in diluted DES systems. This multi-faceted approach allows us to correlate molecular-level changes with macroscopic properties like extraction efficiency, provid-ing a more holistic understanding of the system's behavior across a wide range of water contents. These findings provide valuable insights into designing and applying DES-based solvents for extracting bioactive com-pounds. In summary, instead of considering water merely as an innocent diluent, it should be recognized as an active component that influences the solvation environment, the molecular structure of the solvent and as an agent that could hinder the solvent properties (as an extracting me-dia, for instance). The insights presented in this contribution refine the understanding of the water-induced structural transition in DESs and provide a more comprehensive view of the water–DES network, which is especially relevant for applications requiring highly diluted systems. Future research should emphasize the role of water content in other DES formulations and model compounds, further improving our understand-ing of hydration limits in deep eutectic solvent applications.
